title: Toolkit: Cards and Templates for Commerce Architecture Decisions
basis: Reconstructed on 2026-11-13 from the published page (posts/toolkit/index.md) and its former spec.md, whose Non-goals, Open questions, Decision log, Sources and Changelog are carried over. One spec paragraph per unit of the page, in its order; tables are recorded as evidence of the paragraph they follow. Intent, acceptance criteria and role are copied unchanged from journal-spec.json; the journal spec gives a reference page no thesis, so the thesis here is the page's own and only orders its sections. A light pass for a lookup page: entries were checked for consistency with the ledger and rulings, not rewritten.

know: The sixteen cards and templates, the question each answers and the chapter that teaches it.
That every card names an owner, a system of record and a date, and that the cards meet at the entity–owner table.
can_do: Pick the card for the question on their desk, copy its fields and fill it with their own facts.
Keep the cards current: review on a calendar, let incidents add fields, drop fields nobody reads.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a question from their own work, the reader picks the card that answers it and the chapter that teaches it.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this page: a vendor has announced a new API version for the flow that sends stock to a marketplace, and support sees three different statuses for one order. Which cards do you fill in, which chapters teach them, and which three fields does every card carry?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Tool 4, the integration contract card (api-contracts-and-versioning), for the new version; Tool 7, the order state card (order-management), for the statuses. Every card names an owner, a system of record and a date.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader explains how the cards connect and what a decision record must name.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this page: which record do the other cards meet at, and what must an architecture decision record state beyond Nygard's original fields?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The entity–owner table: a decision record names the ownership rows it changes, and a contract card names its integration inventory row; a fact with no row or a row with no owner is the problem. The decision record adds Ownership (the entity–owner rows whose owner or writer changes), Vendors (contracts, API versions and exit terms it depends on), Confirmation (how conformance is checked) and Review (a date or trigger).

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict what the page contains and the kind of evidence or material it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this page give you, in what order, and from what kind of material?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Sixteen cards that make undecided owners and recovery visible by recording the business fact, the owner, the systems involved and the expected result, from a capability map to a migration plan and a decision record, each with instructions and a linked chapter; examples filled with fictional Kestrel & Pine facts to be replaced; three conventions: keep cards with the work, link them by identifier, investigate consequential blanks.

thesis.question: Which cards and templates do the chapters introduce, and where is each one used?
thesis.claim: Sixteen cards, one per recurring question, each taken from the chapter that teaches it and naming an owner, a system of record and a date, let a reader record a decision without rereading the chapter; they meet at the entity–owner table, so a change to one row says which other cards to update.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that templates belong in a team's own tools and a book needs only the reasoning, so a gathered set of cards duplicates the chapters.
thesis.so_what: A reader with a question from their own work picks one card, copies its fields and fills it with their facts, and knows which other cards a change touches.
thesis.how_why: Each card's fields come from the chapter that teaches it, are filled once with ledger facts, and cite each other by identifier through the entity–owner table.

supporting_claims.claim: A question from the reader's work leads through one table to the card that answers it and the chapter that teaches it.
Each card states its purpose, its fields, how to use it and one filled Kestrel & Pine example, and names an owner, a system of record and a date.
The cards meet at the entity–owner table, so a change to one row tells the reader which other cards to update.

role.contribution: Gives the part the working records: one card per recurring question, so a decision taught in a chapter can be recorded without rereading it.

flow.rationale: The lookup table and the map of connections come first, so a reader arriving with a question finds the card and sees where it sits before reading any card. The sixteen cards follow in the order of the chapters that teach them, from the capability map to the decision record, which changes rows in all the others; the closing says how to keep them current.

hook.content: A design discussion can end with agreement about a new system while leaving its data owner or recovery process undecided.

bridge.from_reader_world: The reader has met cards in the chapters, each introduced where it was needed, and now has a question from their own work.
bridge.to_topic: This page gathers the sixteen cards for lookup, each with a filled example and its chapter.

thesis_statement.text: Every card names an owner, a system of record and a date; the cards point at each other; most fields were paid for by an incident.

conclusion.heading: Keeping the Cards True
conclusion.synthesis: The cards stay useful only while they match the systems, so the same owner-and-date discipline that fills them also keeps them current.
conclusion.so_what: A stale card is worse than none because readers trust it; three habits keep the set current and small.

callback.to: The KEY POINT that most fields were paid for by an incident.
callback.how: Incidents keep adding fields, and fields nobody reads are removed.

takeaway.content: Review each card on its calendar, add a field when an incident asks a question no card answers, and drop fields nobody reads.

decision_log.decision: Converted spec.md to spec.json in a light pass for a lookup page: one spec paragraph per draft unit, tables as evidence; the old inventory-style success criteria were not carried over (the journal spec's acceptance criteria replace them). length.max_words is the published length plus 10%.
rejected: Specifying each table row as a paragraph
Carrying the old success criteria over

decision_log.decision: After draft-check round 1 (REVISE), applied the cheap fixes only, with no second round: the introduction puts the motivation before the instruction and glosses Waypoint, W1-W8 = KP-001-KP-008, Duiven, Eva, the marketplaces and the newcomer abbreviations (WMS, OMS, PIM, PSP, EDI, SKU) with a glossary pointer; 'write unknown' moved to the conventions; KEY POINTS field names match the templates; Tool 3's first-person 'I would adopt' made impersonal; bol, Eva, the Tiel 3PL and hero SKUs glossed in place; Tool 12 shows rung 4, which Tool 9 cites (chapter journey-peak-day's ladder); Tool 16 names confirmation among the ADR's additions (AC-2); the closing says why a stale card matters.
rejected: A second check round (the brief allows one)
Splitting Tool 5's how-to paragraph, which would change the unit count and the spec

decision_log.decision: Consistency fixes only: the stock sync chain in Tool 6 is 'up to two hours end to end' with no hop intervals (scenario-ledger line 71; RESOLVE rule 1); Tool 7's invoice trigger is one invoice per shipment with no per-order alternative (consistency ruling 18); Tool 13's Belgian e-invoicing row hedges whether the mandate binds a Dutch supplier (rulings 5 and 17, chapter 36's row); KP-004 and Tool 1 say 'the shop platform' (RESOLVE rule 11); the first sentence of the introduction now says what the page is for and how to use it; the Tool 2 example table, whose last row had a sentence fused into it, was split into the table and a following sentence.

The former open question on unowned integrations is settled by consistency ruling 16 (13 of 34 in January 2027, 5 in April 2027); the page states neither count, so nothing changes. The glossary hand-off resolves now that the glossary exists.
Put the entity–owner table at the center of the 'How the Records Connect' diagram, because every other card fills, changes or reads one of its rows.
